name: Dâu Pagoda
summary: One of the oldest Buddhist centres in Vietnam, in the old citadel of Luy Lâu. It is dedicated to the goddess of clouds and rain.

eras.label: c. 200 CE
eras.title: Buddhism comes to Luy Lâu
eras.text: Around the 2nd and 3rd centuries, monks from India and Central Asia came to Luy Lâu, then the capital of Chinese-ruled Giao Chỉ. They translated sutras and built some of the first Buddhist temples in the region.

image.alt: A Buddhist statue at Dâu Pagoda

eras.title: Rebuilt under the Trần
eras.text: In 1313 the scholar Mạc Đĩnh Chi rebuilt the pagoda on a grand scale, with halls, galleries and a tower. Much of today's layout follows that plan.

eras.label: Lê dynasty
eras.title: The Hòa Phong tower
eras.text: The brick tower of Hòa Phong, which stands at the entrance, dates from the Lê dynasty. Only three of its storeys have survived the centuries.

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Prayers for rain
eras.text: The pagoda is still active. Its statue of Pháp Vân, the goddess of clouds, is carried in procession during the Dâu festival on the 8th day of the fourth lunar month.

image.alt: The main hall of Dâu Pagoda

story.title: The goddesses of cloud, rain, thunder and lightning
story.narration: Long ago, the legend says, a young woman named Man Nương lived near Luy Lâu and served an Indian monk called Khâu Đà La. She gave birth to a daughter, whom the monk placed inside a hollow tree. Years later, a storm brought the tree down into the river, and it floated to the citadel. People carved it into four statues: the goddesses of clouds, rain, thunder and lightning. The four pagodas that house them have been prayed to for rain ever since. Dâu Pagoda holds Pháp Vân, the goddess of clouds.

story.title: Luy Lâu, the first city
story.narration: Two thousand years ago, the citadel of Luy Lâu stood here, surrounded by earthen walls. It was the seat of the Chinese governors of Giao Chỉ, the best known being Shi Xie (Sĩ Nhiếp in Vietnamese), who ruled around 200 CE. Merchants arrived by river and by sea, and with them came Buddhist monks from India. Some historians think Luy Lâu was a centre of Buddhism even before the faith became widespread in China. Traces of the old walls can still be seen near the pagoda.

story.title: Quan họ: songs across the water

image.file: Trung tâm văn hóa Kinh Bắc.jpg

story.narration: Quan họ is sung by pairs of men and women, called liền anh and liền chị, from different villages. They answer each other in song, matching tune and rhyme, sometimes from boats on a pond. The singers wear traditional dress: turbans and long gowns for the men, and wide flat hats and layered áo tứ thân for the women. There are hundreds of melodies. At the Lim festival each spring, the hillside and the ponds fill with singers.

do: Cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your hat inside the halls.
Walk around the main altar quietly, and let worshippers go first.
Visit the Đông Hồ woodblock print village on the same day.
dont: Point your feet at the altars or sit on temple steps in front of them.
Photograph people who are praying without asking.

tips.title: Local food
tips.text: Try bánh phu thê (sticky "husband and wife" cakes), and Lục Ngạn lychees in June.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 1 hour by car from Hà Nội.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: Bút Tháp Pagoda, with its famous thousand-armed Bodhisattva statue, and the Đông Hồ print village.
